newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thai stocks plunge in mixed day for Asian markets.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks plunge in mixed day for Asian markets.

text.p: Thai stocks fell to their lowest level in nearly three years on Monday as brokerages were forced to unload stocks held by clients unable to top up margin loans, brokers said.
The Bangkok bourse was the worst performing Asian market of the day, with the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index losing 2.1 percent after having fallen nearly nine percent last week.
Thai investors were uninspired by Wall Street's strong gain on Friday after U.S. employment figures came in roughly as expected, easing fears of a strong rate rise in the short term.

Elsewhere on Monday, Hong Kong stocks staged a healthy rebound, more than recouping last week's losses, while South Korean shares gained more than 1.5 per cent and Tokyo's Nikkei continued to rise further from the key 20,000 point level.
Thai stocks closed below the 1,000-point level, their lowest since September 30, 1993, continuing last week's sell-off.
The market was savaged by selling last Thursday and Friday on rumours that some brokerages might be hit by client defaults on margin loans.
Sentiment was also hurt by the news on Tuesday that Moody's Investors Service had downgraded Thailand's short-term debt ratings, and by higher oil prices after the United States attacked Iraq.
The index fell sharply late in the session on Monday after about 10 finance stocks hit the 10 percent limit lows, followed by property, energy and building issues, brokers said.
The index finished down 21.19 points at 986.32. On September 30, 1993, the index closed at 971.44.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 187.01 points, or 1.70 percent, to 11,212.60, but low turnover suggested many investors remained cautious on the near term outlook, brokers said.
"Last week, the market was discounting a larger rise in interest rates, said Kieran Hung, vice-president, institutional sales at G.K. Goh Securities.
The market fell 1.2 percent last week, fearing that any stronger than expected rise in U.S. employment could prompt the Fed to raise rates aggressively from this month.
But the jobless rate fell to 5.1 percent in August, and non-farm payrolls rose by 250,000, about even with economists' estimates.
"Because of the U.S. election, we are not expecting more than a 25 basis-point hike," Hung said.

Tokyo stocks closed mixed after an early morning rally, sparked by the August U.S. employment data, fizzled out, brokers said. The key 225-share Nikkei average closed up 49.74 points, or 0.25 percent, at 20,202.27.
"The rebound was extremely slow, indicating that it is still possible for stocks to post more losses," said Harushige Kobayashi, an analyst at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.

Brokers in Seoul said that Monday's 1.54 percent rise was due to institutional investors managing their portfolios ahead of October's rise in the foreign shareholding ceiling to 20 percent. The composite index rose 12.12 points to a provisional close of 797.38.

The dollar dipped slightly by late Monday Tokyo trade, but the downside was holding on listless trade. The dollar was stuck near 109.10/20 yen before falling to 108.89/99 yen by 1120 GMT in European trade.

SIMEX Brent futures were mixed in late trading, but geared to the downside as the market continued to cool down after last week's missile attacks on Iraq. October Brent was traded at $22.55 per barrel, up one cent from London's close on Friday.
Hong Kong gold ended at US$384.90/385.40 an ounce against New York's US$384.85/385.35 close on Friday.
